parts.shows: Write, break, fix — and find out which Python
parts.why: Until a file you wrote runs on your machine, nothing else here works. A1 asks whether you can read code, run it and fix it, so you do all three in the first hour, on three lines you wrote yourself. Nobody warns you about the last part. python3 is a name, not a file, and your shell has to look it up. On a Mac it can find more than one.

predict.ask: You have more than one Python installed. When you type python3, one of them runs. If you use that one to build a virtual environment, which Python is in the environment?
options: The newest one on the machine. A fresh environment should give you a fresh Python.
The one you built it with.

parts.receipt_prompt: Paste both architecture answers, commands and all — what uname -m said, and what platform.machine() said from inside your environment.

compare.note: A virtual environment uses the Python you built it with. It does not search for a better one. The measured reference comes from the original setup: an Apple-silicon machine running Intel Python 3.12, with native Python 3.9 also installed. An environment made from that first Python inherited its Intel architecture. Your answers may differ. If both say arm64, that architecture mismatch is absent; check the Python version separately. which python3 shows the first match; which -a python3 shows them all.
compare.after: Use a native Python 3.12 from here on. The course has its own, and what follows sets this terminal up to use it. Then ask the two architecture questions again.

concepts.anchor: Like a folder-specific copy of a tool, rather than a search for the newest tool.
concepts.explain: A virtual environment keeps the Python it was created from. It does not look for a newer one, and it does not look for one that suits this machine better.

concepts.anchor: Like checking drawers in a fixed order and using the first matching tool.
concepts.explain: PATH is an ordered list of folders. The shell looks in them one by one and runs the first match. which python3 names that match, and which -a python3 lists them all.

parts.brief: An agent wrote this script from one sentence: “a script that checks my setup”. It runs, and it ends by printing Success.
questions: Before you read it: if someone says “my Python setup is fine”, what would have to be true? Name the things a check would have to look at.
Still before you open it: what would you expect a script like this to tell you, and what could it leave out?
Now walk through it. It prints the same Success line whether the report worked or not. Say what that costs you, and name the one line you would change first.
looks_for: Which interpreter answers, where it is, what version and architecture it is, and what is installed in it — several facts, not one.

A script like this reports on the Python that is running the script — which need not be the python3 your terminal finds — and it can easily say nothing about what is installed. Question 3 is where you see what this one does.

That the same Success line prints whether the report worked or raised, so the word carries no information; the line to change is the except Exception that swallows the failure, which should let it through or say what failed.

sessions.title: Order and state
sessions.subtitle: Six rows arrive in an order, and a count has to survive the loop. SQL never asked you where to put the counter.

parts.shows: Loop over six rows, count some, keep a running total
parts.why: A1’s own check describes a script an agent wrote: it turns a two-million-row export into a weekly revenue table, prints Success every run, and this week’s total jumped 12% with no business reason. The middle of that script is a loop that keeps a number while it walks the rows. Where that number is set decides what the total ends up being — and neither version fails, so nothing tells you which one you have. You write that loop here, on six rows you can check by eye.
parts.setup: Six rows are waiting in a file called rows.py: each one a name, a team and an amount. You will fetch that file, write a loop over the rows at the bottom of it, count some of them, and keep one number that has to last the whole loop. The rows never change.

compare.note: Where you put total = 0 is not a style choice. It is a different answer. SQL never asked you where to put it, because there is no “where”: SUM(amount) is one statement over a set that has no order.
compare.after: The third task needs the total to survive the loop. If nothing ever passes 50, the largest single amount is 31 — so the total is being thrown away each time round.

labels: I had it right, and for the right reason.
I read the loop the way I read SQL: the whole set at once, with no order.
I thought setting it to zero again was the same as leaving it alone.
I expected Python to object to setting the same name twice.
I had it right, but was not sure why.

concepts.anchor: Like a running tally on paper: each time you write a new number the old one is gone, and only the last one is there at the end.
concepts.explain: A name holds one value at a time, and assigning to it replaces what was there. The loop body runs once per row of data, so an assignment inside the body runs once per row too.

concepts.anchor: Like a bank statement: the balance on each line depends on every line above it. A SQL SUM has no “above”.
concepts.explain: The rows come in a sequence and a running total depends on it. “Which row did the total first pass 50 at” has no answer without an order.

sessions.title: Naming and boundaries
sessions.subtitle: A function has its own names. Ten programs to run; eight of them stop.

parts.shows: Read ten broken programs — and the two that are worse than broken
parts.why: An agent hands you two hundred lines. The ones that stop tell you where they stopped, and A1 asks whether you can read that trail and explain every line. The ones that do not stop tell you nothing at all — and two of these ten are that kind: a total that is not the number you asked for, and a column of whole numbers that silently wrapped round to a negative. That is the shape of the script in A1’s own check, the one that prints Success on every run while the week’s total is 12% out.
parts.setup: Ten small programs are waiting. Most are about functions: what a function’s own names are, what it hands back, and what it can reach. Eight of them stop. Two of them finish and print something wrong. You will run all ten, and the sorting is yours to do.

compare.mine_label: Measured reference: the two that did not stop
compare.mine: $ python3 09_money.py charged: 0.30000000000000004 is it 0.30? False $ python3 10_overflow.py before: 2147483647 after one more: -2147483648
compare.theirs_label: Measured reference: what the caller sees
compare.note: A name inside a function belongs to the function. Assigning to it points the function’s own name somewhere new, and the caller never sees that. Changing that object in place, as append does, changes the one object both names point at. What crosses out of a function is what you return, plus anything you changed in place.
compare.after: And the two that did not stop are the expensive kind. 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact form in binary, so their sum is not 0.30 and the comparison is False — which is why money is held in whole cents, or in Decimal, never in a float. The column of whole numbers was already at its type’s ceiling; one more wrapped it round to a negative, with no warning, and the program still ended as if nothing was wrong. The eight that stop tell you the file and the line. These two are the ones you will actually meet.

concepts.explain: Assigning to a variable name inside a function moves only the function’s own name, and the code that called it never sees that. Changing the object itself in place changes the one object both of them hold. Otherwise the only way out is return.

concepts.anchor: Like thirds in decimal: 0.333… never closes, however many digits you write.
concepts.explain: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so their sum is slightly above 0.3 and == returns False. Hold money in whole cents, or in Decimal.

parts.brief: An agent wrote this function from one sentence: “apply the discounts to a price”. Called three times with the same price, it printed 90.0, then 81.0, then 72.9.
questions: Before you read it: someone asks for “apply the discounts to a price”. What has to be true of the answer, and what would you want to see to believe it?
Still before you open it: what could make three calls with the same price give three different answers?
Now walk through it. Name the line that makes the second call different from the first, and say what you would change about how the price itself is held.
looks_for: A price with the discounts applied, and the same price in gives the same price out — calling it twice must not change anything.
Something is being kept from one call to the next: a list or a total that lives outside any single call and is added to each time. Code like this can carry what earlier calls did into later ones.

The default list is made once, when the function is defined, and discounts.append(0.1) adds to that same list on every call that does not pass its own — that is the line. And the price is a float: these three happen to come out clean, but money belongs in whole cents or Decimal, and other prices will not: 1.10 comes back as 0.9900000000000001.
